pharm: Human IgG1 kappa monoclonal antibody that binds CD38 on myeloma and other cells, triggering immune-mediated cell death (ADCC, ADCP, CDC), direct apoptosis, and modulation of CD38 enzymatic activity.
tags: Interferes with blood compatibility testing & M-protein assays
quick: Multiple myeloma: 16 mg/kg IV - weekly wk 1-8, every 2 weeks wk 9-24, then every 4 weeks (varies by regimen)
May cause fetal harm (IgG1 crosses placenta; depletes fetal CD38+ cells); use effective contraception
No data on milk transfer; decision should weigh benefits against risk to infant
No formal dose adjustment studied (population PK suggests none needed)
No formal dose adjustment studied; limited data in moderate/severe impairment
Type & screen BEFORE first dose; CBC (neutrophils, platelets), infusion reactions, HBV status
summary: Daratumumab is a human anti-CD38 IgG1 kappa monoclonal antibody approved for multiple myeloma across multiple lines of therapy (in various combinations and as monotherapy) and, in its subcutaneous co-formulation with hyaluronidase (Darzalex Faspro), for newly diagnosed light-chain (AL) amyloidosis. The intravenous formulation (Darzalex) is dosed at 16 mg/kg, typically weekly for weeks 1-8, every 2 weeks for weeks 9-24, then every 4 weeks thereafter, with the exact schedule varying by regimen. Patients must receive pre-infusion and post-infusion medications (corticosteroid, antipyretic, antihistamine) to reduce infusion-related reactions, which are common - mostly with the first infusion - and managed by interrupting or slowing the infusion. Daratumumab binds CD38 on red blood cells, causing a positive indirect antiglobulin test (indirect Coombs) that interferes with blood compatibility testing for up to 6 months, so type and screen patients BEFORE starting. It also interferes with serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation used to monitor M-protein. Other key risks are neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, and hepatitis B virus reactivation.
indications: Multiple myeloma - in combination regimens for newly diagnosed disease (transplant-eligible and transplant-ineligible patients)
Multiple myeloma - in combination regimens for relapsed/refractory disease (after one or more prior lines of therapy)
Multiple myeloma - as monotherapy in patients who have received at least three prior lines including a proteasome inhibitor and an immunomodulatory agent, or who are double-refractory to both
Newly diagnosed light-chain (AL) amyloidosis - subcutaneous co-formulation (daratumumab + hyaluronidase, Darzalex Faspro) in combination with bortezomib, cyclophosphamide, and dexamethasone

dosage.t: Weeks 1-8 weekly (weeks 1-2 of cycles in some regimens)

admin: Determine ABO/Rh blood type and perform a red cell antibody screen (type & screen) BEFORE the first dose, because daratumumab interferes with subsequent compatibility testing
Premedicate before each infusion: corticosteroid, antipyretic (acetaminophen), and antihistamine; give post-infusion corticosteroid (especially after the first infusions) to reduce delayed reactions
Administer IV only after dilution in sodium chloride 0.9%; start at the recommended (slow) initial rate and escalate as tolerated per labeling
Have resuscitation equipment available; interrupt or slow the infusion for infusion-related reactions and resume at a reduced rate after symptoms resolve
Consider antiviral prophylaxis (e.g., for herpes zoster) and screen for hepatitis B before initiation; co-administer per the specific combination regimen
moa: Daratumumab is a human IgG1 kappa monoclonal antibody that binds with high affinity to CD38, a glycoprotein highly expressed on multiple myeloma cells. By engaging CD38, it kills tumor cells through multiple immune-mediated mechanisms - complement-dependent cytotoxicity (CDC), antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC), and antibody-dependent cellular phagocytosis (ADCP) - as well as by inducing direct apoptosis via Fc-mediated crosslinking. It also modulates CD38 enzymatic (ectoenzyme) activity and depletes CD38-positive immunosuppressive regulatory cells, enhancing antitumor immune responses. Because CD38 is also expressed at low levels on red blood cells, daratumumab binding produces serologic test interference.

absolute: History of severe hypersensitivity (e.g., anaphylaxis) to daratumumab or any component of the formulation (including hyaluronidase in the SC co-formulation)
relative: Active hepatitis B infection or HBV carrier status (reactivation risk - screen and monitor)
History of obstructive pulmonary disease (e.g., COPD, asthma) - higher risk of severe infusion-related bronchospasm; consider additional post-infusion medications
Pregnancy and women of reproductive potential not using effective contraception
monitor: Complete blood count - particularly neutrophil and platelet counts - periodically during therapy
Signs and symptoms of infusion-related reactions throughout and after each infusion
Hepatitis B reactivation (HBV DNA and clinical signs) during and after treatment
Indirect antiglobulin (Coombs) interference - ensure blood bank is informed before transfusion

preg: Daratumumab may cause fetal harm. As a human IgG1 antibody it crosses the placenta and may cause fetal myeloid- or lymphoid-cell depletion and reduced bone density by depleting CD38-positive immune cells. There are no adequate human data, and combination partners (e.g., lenalidomide, thalidomide) may themselves be teratogenic. Advise women of reproductive potential to use effective contraception during treatment and for 3 months after the last dose.
lact: There is no information on the presence of daratumumab in human milk, its effects on the breastfed infant, or on milk production. Human IgG is present in milk; the developmental and health benefits of breastfeeding should be weighed against the mother's clinical need for daratumumab and any potential adverse effects on the infant from the drug or the underlying condition.
renal: No formal dose-adjustment studies were conducted. Population pharmacokinetic analyses indicate that renal impairment does not meaningfully alter daratumumab exposure, and no dosage adjustment is recommended based on renal function.
hepatic: No formal dedicated hepatic-impairment studies were conducted. Population pharmacokinetic data suggest mild hepatic impairment does not meaningfully affect exposure; data in moderate to severe hepatic impairment are limited, but no specific dosage adjustment is recommended.

major: Live or live-attenuated vaccines - avoid during treatment because of immunosuppression and impaired vaccine response/infection risk
moderate: Other myelosuppressive agents (chemotherapy, lenalidomide, bortezomib, corticosteroids in regimen) - additive neutropenia/thrombocytopenia; monitor counts and adjust supportive care
Concomitant immunosuppressants - additive infection risk including HBV reactivation
minor: No clinically significant small-molecule cytochrome P450 pharmacokinetic interactions established for this monoclonal antibody
interactions.diagnostics: Daratumumab binds CD38 on red blood cells and produces a POSITIVE INDIRECT ANTIGLOBULIN TEST (indirect Coombs), interfering with red cell antibody screening and blood compatibility testing (crossmatch) for up to 6 months after the last dose - type and screen patients BEFORE starting therapy and notify the blood bank; reagents (e.g., dithiothreitol-treated cells) or genotyping/phenotyping can mitigate this, but Kell antigen is destroyed by DTT (give K-negative units). Daratumumab is itself an IgG kappa antibody and can be detected on SERUM PROTEIN ELECTROPHORESIS (SPEP) and IMMUNOFIXATION, causing a false-positive IgG kappa band that may confound assessment of complete response/M-protein monitoring.

common: Infusion-related reactions (chills, fever, cough, nasal congestion, dyspnea, throat tightness - mostly with the first infusion)
Peripheral edema and peripheral neuropathy (in combination regimens)
serious: Severe/serious infusion-related reactions including bronchospasm, hypoxia, dyspnea, hypertension, laryngeal edema
Neutropenia (including febrile neutropenia) with increased infection risk
Serious infections including pneumonia and sepsis
Hepatitis B virus reactivation (can be fatal)
Second primary malignancies (in some combination settings)
rare: Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES, reported with combination regimens)
emergency: Anaphylaxis or severe infusion reaction with airway compromise/hypoxia
Acute hepatic failure from HBV reactivation

monitoring: Type and screen (ABO/Rh and red cell antibody screen) BEFORE the first dose; inform blood bank of daratumumab use before any transfusion
Complete blood count periodically during therapy - monitor absolute neutrophil count and platelets; manage with dose delays/growth factors/transfusion as needed
Observe closely for infusion-related reactions during and after each infusion (especially the first); ensure premedication is given
Screen for hepatitis B (HBsAg, anti-HBc) before therapy and monitor for reactivation during and after treatment
Monitor response with awareness that daratumumab interferes with SPEP/immunofixation (may need daratumumab-specific reflex assay to confirm complete response)
counsel: Reactions during the infusion (chills, fever, cough, shortness of breath, throat tightness, stuffy nose) are common, especially the first time - tell your nurse immediately; the infusion can be slowed or paused and pre-medications help prevent them
Carry a card or alert noting you receive daratumumab: it interferes with blood-bank testing for up to 6 months, so any hospital giving you a transfusion must know
Report fever, sore throat, or signs of infection promptly because this drug can lower your white cells and platelets - also report unusual bruising or bleeding
Use effective birth control during treatment and for 3 months after the last dose; do not breastfeed without discussing with your doctor
Avoid live vaccines while on therapy and tell your doctor about any history of hepatitis B or breathing problems such as asthma/COPD
pk: Concentration-dependent CD38-mediated cytotoxicity; clinical response over weeks of dosing
Trough concentrations rise through the weekly dosing phase, approaching steady state near the end of weekly dosing
~18 days at steady state (concentration-dependent, target-mediated clearance)
Long exposure; serologic (Coombs) interference can persist up to ~6 months after the last dose
Refrigerate vials at 2-8 C (36-46 F); protect from light; do not freeze or shake; dilute in 0.9% sodium chloride before infusion
pearls: INFUSION-RELATED REACTIONS occur in a large proportion of patients - mostly during the FIRST infusion; mandatory pre- and post-infusion medications (corticosteroid, antipyretic, antihistamine) plus interrupting/slowing the infusion are the cornerstone of management; consider montelukast/short-acting bronchodilators in patients with obstructive lung disease

SEROLOGIC INTERFERENCE: daratumumab binds CD38 on RBCs causing a positive indirect Coombs that confounds crossmatch/antibody screen for up to 6 months - TYPE AND SCREEN BEFORE the first dose and alert the blood bank (DTT-treated reagent cells help but destroy Kell - give K-negative blood)

M-PROTEIN INTERFERENCE: daratumumab (IgG kappa) shows up on SPEP and immunofixation and can mimic residual M-protein, potentially masking a true complete response - a daratumumab-specific reflex assay may be needed
Monitor for and manage NEUTROPENIA and THROMBOCYTOPENIA; screen for and monitor HEPATITIS B reactivation before and during therapy

Darzalex (IV, 16 mg/kg weight-based) is distinct from Darzalex Faspro (subcutaneous fixed-dose daratumumab + hyaluronidase, 1800 mg) - the SC form has lower infusion-reaction rates, shorter administration time, and is the form approved (in combination) for AL amyloidosis
missed: If a planned dose is missed, administer it as soon as possible and adjust the subsequent dosing schedule to maintain the treatment interval, per the prescribing regimen. Daratumumab is given in a clinical setting, so missed or delayed doses should be rescheduled by the oncology team rather than self-managed.
overdose: There is no known specific antidote for daratumumab overdose, and no established maximum tolerated dose was identified in clinical trials. In the event of overdose, monitor the patient closely for any signs or symptoms of adverse reactions (particularly infusion-related reactions and cytopenias) and institute appropriate supportive and symptomatic treatment immediately.
